Rents Due

By: Harri Vithi | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

Unique Selling Point:
This story:
Exposes false scarcity
Challenges the idea that government failure is accidental


Summary:
This story says:

People are homeless not because the state lacks resources — but because those resources are redirected.

In July 2024, newly appointed Public Works and Infrastructure Minister Dean Macpherson vowed to drastically reduce government’s reliance on leasing private buildings.

Yet last year, four new leases worth R290 million were approved — despite the department sitting with a R30 billion maintenance backlog and owning hundreds of underutilised properties.
Public Works says more than 800 lease requests were denied, raising a critical question:

Why does leasing still appear to be the default — even when the state already owns buildings that could be refurbished and occupied?

Nowhere is this contradiction more stark than in Gauteng.

In April 2025, public outrage erupted over the Gauteng Provincial Government’s R34 million monthly rental bill for 11 privately owned buildings — amounting to R408 million a year.

Premier Panyaza Lesufi publicly expressed shock, saying he was unaware of the expenditure, and announced an independent probe, promising a report within two months.


Further information:
It is now January 2025, and the status as well as findings of that investigation have not been made public.

What complicates matters further is that the Office of the Premier itself is among the tenants, paying just over R4 million a month — rivalled only by the Department of Agriculture.

An analysis of the lease agreements shows that at least R 14 million of the R34 million monthly rental can be traced back to one businessman and his companies: Herbert Seabelo Theledi, a property magnate with a reported R2 billion portfolio. This is disproportionate as no other lessor comes close in terms of rental income.

While there is nothing unlawful about private enterprise, several of the lease agreements involving Theledi’s companies have previously been flagged in media and political reports as irregular or politically connected, including allegations relating to an ANC front company and a R27 million payment made via the Johannesburg Property Company.

Theledi has also been linked to:

A R448 million lease tender alleged to have been rigged

A long-running corruption case dating back to the 2010 FIFA World Cup, involving the Mbombela Stadium project, which remains unresolved more than a decade later

The broader impact is not abstract.

Script:


(Claire) It has been almost a year since the Gauteng Province committed to investigating its own building leases.

(Claire) Because every month, the province pays around thirty-four million rand in rent to private landlords — when its own buildings stand empty.

(Claire )This building is owned by the Gauteng Province and it's not in use.

(Claire) The buildings’ proximity is not a coincidence.

(Claire) They were meant to form part of a single government precinct and from what I can see nothing much is happening here either.
(Claire) Joburg’s Kopanong Precinct was conceptualized in 2003 as a sort of headquarters for various Gauteng government departments. Almost R200 million has been spent on rates and taxes over the past 5 years. Yet, the buildings are largely empty and falling apart.
(Claire) Imagine buying a house, leaving it empty - and opting to rent another house to live in. Well that's exactly what the province has chosen to do, repeatedly - at taxpayers expense.
(Claire) In April last year, the DA’s Khathutshero Rasilingwane asked Gauteng’s Infrastructure MEC how many buildings the province leases. The answer: eleven, costing over R400 million a year — it made headlines.
(Khathutshelo Rasilingwane) For me that was quite a shock and on the list it gave us obviously information to say this has been ongoing for the past 10 years. And when you look at it over five years, that is over 2 billion.
(Claire) As the months rolled by with no tangible answers from the Gauteng Province, we began our own investigation.
(Claire) In this voice note, an anonymous informant confirms the pattern - public funds spent on buildings that barely get used.
(Anonymous) Do you remember that building, it’s also the department’s - it’s also unoccupied; it’s barely used - but rent is still being paid.
(Sabelo Chalufu) It's a strange situation. Typically, when you own an asset, you want to use it.
(Claire) Governance expert Sabelo Chalufu has experience in state property management.
(Sabelo Chalufu) It raises some questions around why did you actually purchase such an asset in the first place
(Sabelo Chalufu) In the event they are not using, it's most likely you'll find that they are then leasing accommodation elsewhere.
(Claire) I mean is there any reasonable explanation?


(Sabelo Chalufu) What you actually find when you go below the surface is that there is typically some abuse of the system.
(Claire) Given the province’s 41 empty buildings, all the private leases require some examination, and one set in particular stands out.
(Khathutshelo Rasilingwane) From the 11 rented buildings or the leases, six of the buildings belong to one individual.
(Claire) And that businessman is Herbert Theledi.
(Claire) Across these leases, his companies receive the largest share. By April last year, that amounted to R13.5 million a month — that’s R162 million a year. Herbert Theledi, it seems, is well-versed in government contracts.
(Sabelo Chalufu) Because the commercial property sector is high value but the cost of entry is so high, there's actually a small group of people and businesses that operate there.
(Claire) Why is that problematic for you?

(Khathutshelo Rasilingwane) Realistically, when you consider the procurement processes, it's often deemed to be a red flag for us.

(Claire) Rasilingwane says the City refuses to share all the lease agreements.


(Sabelo Chalufu) It then causes alarm in the sense that what is it that you're hiding?


( Claire) So, we dig deeper. His websites describe Herbert Theledi as a visionary leader with over 35 years in real estate, and property portfolios valued at over R2 billion.
(Claire) And behind some of these leases, troubling questions emerge.
(Claire) In 2022, Herbert Theledi’s name was connected to a building called Proton House leased to the City of Johannesburg. A controversy previously featured on Carte Blanche.


(Leah Knott) It was decrepit, the lifts didn’t work - the doors were broken.


(Claire) Our anonymous source has inside knowledge of the lease.


(Anonymous) The building was leased from Herbert Theledi’s company but Herbert does not own the building, the building is owned by Investec Bank.


(Claire) For 16 years, the City had leased the building from an Investec subsidiary. Then, despite not owning the building, Theledi’s company, Bertocure, took over the lease in 2017.
(Claire) Four years later, Bertocure sued the City, primarily over damage to the property and arrears in rent, and eventually received nearly R24 million.


(Anonymous) Why is the City paying a middleman for a building that the middleman does not own?


(Claire) Then there were allegations from opposition parties that Bertocure was an ANC-linked front and that the payout was used to fund elections.


(Claire) The lease was investigated by the City, but we’ve been told by the company, responsible for managing Joburg’s publicly owned properties, that they’re not aware of any corruption between their officials and Theledi.
(Claire) Investec confirms there was an agreement for its subsidiary to sell Proton House to Bertocure, which could then lease the property to the City. The sale was later cancelled by mutual agreement and , Bertocure paid part of the settlement to the subsidiary. Proton House hasn’t yet been restored.
(Khathutshelo Rasilingwane) From the 11 buildings that are currently being used, we then found out that one of them was actually not being utilized.

(Claire) Our source says this rental stood empty for part of the nine years it was rented to the Province.
(Claire) The address: 55 Fox Street, the landlord: Herbert Theledi’s - Shenge Property Group.


(Khathutshelo Rasilingwane) We were informed because it's unsafe. There's water issues, there's electricity issues.


(Claire) Despite alleged health and safety concerns, last year Infrastructure MEC, Jacob Mamabolo, said the province was obliged to continue paying Theledi’s company until the lease expired in September.


(Claire) Allegedly, the Department of Education mostly used it for printing.
(Sabelo Chalufu) What kind of printing are you doing in a building that is costing you almost R 3 million. It is such a strange thing.
(Khathutshelo Rasilingwane) Why this specific individual, why getting 6 out of the 11 contracts and what’s so special about the buildings that they provide? And so we will be going forward and conduct further investigation on this specific company.
(Claire) Gauteng Premier, Panyaza Lesufi’s offices - leased from another landlord - cost taxpayers R 48 million a year.
(Claire) Did the Premier know that his office was costing R 4 million of taxpayers money per month or was he surprised?

(Khathuthselo Rasilingwane) So he went around all the media houses obviously acting shocked and acting as if he was going to act against this whole issue.

(Claire) In April last year, Lesufi promised a forensic report would be released within three months.

(Khathutshelo Rasilingwane) We are in February this year and nothing has happened. We haven't received any report.

(Claire) Meanwhile, the state-owned Office of the Premier stands empty.

(Claire) Another empty building. This time with Premier Panyaza Lesufi’s face on it.

(Claire) The Premier’s office and Gauteng Department of Infrastructure declined interviews, citing an ongoing investigation.
(Claire) There was no response to our questions about the Proton House investigation.
(Claire) Herbert Theledi denies he has a corrupt relationship with the ANC or any government officials. He says all the allegations around his lease agreements with the Gauteng Province and City are defamatory and unsubstantiated, adding that all leases were the result of legal tenders. He says Bertocure’s Proton House settlement was above board. The ANC didn’t respond to our request for comment.
(Claire) Whether it’s paying rent or rates on its own properties, it seems the Province is happy to pay for empty buildings.
